intro: Expressions calculate values and sometimes change stored objects. Learn arithmetic, comparisons, logic, bit operations, and assignment while tracking their operand types and side effects.
outcomes: Distinguish bitwise operations from truth operations.
Recognise invalid arithmetic and unsafe side effects.
prerequisites: An operand is a value an operator acts on. A side effect changes program state, such as assigning a variable. A nonzero scalar value is true in a C condition; zero is false.

sections.title: 1. Arithmetic and comparison
paragraphs: +, -, *, /, and % supply addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and integer remainder. % requires integer operands. Integer division truncates toward zero: -7 / 3 is -2 and -7 % 3 is -1. Division by zero is invalid; signed INT_MIN / -1 is also invalid when the quotient is not representable.

<, <=, >, >=, ==, and != yield int values 0 or 1. = assigns; == compares. Do not write 0 <= x <= 10 for a range: the first comparison yields 0 or 1, which is then compared with 10. Write 0 <= x && x <= 10.

Compound assignment such as total += value updates an object using an operation. ++ increments by one; postfix x++ yields the old value, whereas prefix ++x yields the new value. Prefer standalone updates when the expression would otherwise be difficult to trace.

sections.title: 2. Logic, bits, and conditional selection
paragraphs: && means logical AND, || means logical OR, and ! negates truth. && and || short-circuit: the right operand is evaluated only when needed. denominator != 0 && numerator / denominator > 2 avoids division when the denominator is zero, assuming the other division cases are valid.

&, |, ^, and ~ combine or invert individual integer bits. They do not short-circuit. Use unsigned operands for bit manipulation and valid shift counts. A shift count must be nonnegative and less than the width of the promoted left operand; signed shifts have additional restrictions.

condition ? yes : no evaluates the condition and only the selected result operand. sizeof obtains a size, usually without evaluating its operand, but variable-length-array cases require care. The comma operator sequences its left expression before the right expression; argument-separating commas do not do that.
example: 7/3 is 2 and 7%3 is 1. 5u is binary 101 and 2u is binary 010, so AND=0, OR=7, XOR=7. Postfix increment stores 7 in old and then leaves a=8. The last line prints old=7 now=8 max=8.

sections.title: 3. Side effects and safe expression design
paragraphs: Avoid expressions such as i++ + i++: they contain unsequenced modifications to the same scalar object and have undefined behaviour. Do not guess the output from one compiler. Separate each modification into its own statement.

Address-of &x and dereference *p are unary operators that connect objects and pointers; multiplication and bitwise AND use the same symbols in binary contexts. The syntactic context determines the operation. Arrays and dynamic storage chapters introduce the needed pointer model.

For each expression ask: what are the operand types, what conversions occur, what value is produced, and which objects change? That checklist reveals errors hidden by a correct-looking mathematical formula.

revision: Use && for ranges and guarded operations.
Use unsigned values for bit operations.
Keep updates separate when sequencing is unclear.

questions.question: Why is 0 <= x <= 10 wrong as a range test?
answer: It groups as (0 <= x) <= 10. The first result is 0 or 1, and both are <=10, so it is always true. Use 0 <= x && x <= 10.

questions.question: How do 5 & 2 and 5 && 2 differ?
answer: Bitwise AND combines 101 and 010 and produces 0. Logical AND observes that both numbers are nonzero and produces 1. Logical AND can skip its second operand; bitwise AND evaluates both operands.

questions.question: What is the output of printf("%d %d", i++, i++)?
answer: There is no portable output to predict. The two unsequenced modifications of i cause undefined behaviour. Store each result in separate statements, then print those results.
